Getting Roof Work Done Between the Last Bell and the First

School and university facilities teams in the Triad have one real construction window most years, and it runs from the last day of class to the first. We plan roof projects for K-12 districts and higher-education campuses across Winston-Salem, Davidson, Davie, and Yadkin counties around that window, and we build the rest of our process around procurement rules that public education budgets require.

Who We Work With in School and University Facilities

On a K-12 project the point of contact is usually a district facilities director or an executive director of operations working through a bond program, often alongside a construction management firm the district retained for the bond cycle. Districts across this part of the Piedmont range from Winston-Salem/Forsyth County's larger campuses down to smaller Davie and Yadkin county schools where the facilities office covers every building in the system directly.

Higher education is a different rhythm. A campus facilities office at a school like Wake Forest University, Winston-Salem State University, Salem College, or the Jamestown campus of Guilford Technical Community College is managing research buildings, dormitories, and athletic facilities on staggered academic and research calendars, not a single August-to-June school year.

The Summer Window Problem

A gymnasium reroof cannot start while the building is hosting summer camps or graduation ceremonies, and it has to be closed in, tested, and cleared before band camp or fall athletics move back in. We build the schedule backward from the first day of school, not forward from a contract signing date, and we flag any long-lead membrane or metal panel order early enough that material delays do not eat into the install window.

Higher-education buildings often give us more flexibility, but research space adds its own constraint: a roof over an active lab cannot have vibration or dust intrusion during certain testing windows, so we coordinate directly with the department using the space in addition to the facilities office.

Bond Funding, Bidding, and Procurement Compliance

Most K-12 roof work in North Carolina moves through formal public bid procedures once a project crosses the statutory threshold, and bond-funded work carries its own reporting requirements back to the district's finance office and often to the state. We build our proposals to match that process rather than asking a facilities director to translate a standard commercial quote into public procurement language after the fact.

That means our submittals typically include:

  • Bid-ready specifications matched to the district's or system's procurement format
  • Prevailing wage documentation where the funding source requires it
  • Bonding and insurance certificates sized to the project value
  • Manufacturer warranty terms spelled out for board or bond-committee approval
  • Substantial completion scheduling tied to the academic calendar, not a generic contract date

Board approval cycles add another layer most private commercial clients never deal with. A capital item often has to clear a facilities committee before it reaches the full board agenda, and we time our proposal and pricing validity windows so a district isn't forced to re-bid a project because board scheduling ran long.

Gyms, Auditoriums, and Older Building Stock

Gymnasium and auditorium roofs span farther than a typical classroom wing, which changes the structural deck and fastening pattern conversation before a membrane is even selected. A standing seam metal system is a common fit on these long-span structures, since it sheds the region's summer downpours quickly and holds up over a wide, low-slope span better than some single-ply options. Older schools across the district, some dating to the 1950s and 60s, can carry roof assemblies with asbestos-containing components under later overlays, which changes the tear-off scope and abatement sequencing well before demolition starts.

Portable classrooms added to relieve enrollment pressure bring their own smaller flat or low-slope roofs that get overlooked in a district's capital plan until they start leaking onto instructional space. We include those units in our site assessment rather than treating the main building as the only roof on a campus, and we note them separately in our reporting so a facilities director isn't surprised by a portable roof failure mid-year.

When a Roof Fails During the School Year

Piedmont thunderstorms and the occasional ice event do not wait for summer break. When a roof fails mid-year, the priority shifts from a planned reroof to keeping instructional space dry and safe until the next construction window, usually with an emergency dry-in or targeted repair rather than a full replacement mobilized on short notice.

We document that interim work the same way we document a bond project, with photos, scope notes, and a repair record the district can attach to its own facility file, so the eventual full reroof project has an accurate history instead of a gap in records.

Questions Facilities Directors Ask Us

Can you commit to a hard finish date before school starts?

Yes, and we build the schedule backward from the first day of school rather than forward from a contract date, flagging any long-lead material order early enough to protect that finish date.

Do you handle prevailing wage and bond-program documentation?

We build our bid packages and reporting to match the funding source's requirements, including prevailing wage certification and the paperwork a bond committee or district finance office needs to close out the project.

What happens if a roof leaks during the school year?

We respond with dry-in and interim repair work sized to keep instructional space usable until the next construction window, and we document that work so it feeds into the eventual full reroof scope.

Do older schools need asbestos testing before a reroof?

Buildings from certain decades can carry asbestos-containing roof components under later overlays, so we recommend testing as part of the pre-bid assessment rather than discovering it during tear-off.

How do you handle roof work on an active research building?

We coordinate directly with the department using the space to avoid vibration or dust exposure during sensitive testing windows, in addition to the standard scheduling we run through the campus facilities office.
